title: Quietly working (2 Thessalonians 3:6–13)
hook: work quietly, eat your own bread, don't grow weary in doing well
carry: be not weary in well doing
tomorrow: is money really the root of all evil? read the whole line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rejoice, pray, give thanks: in every thing, not for every thing, and a God who also will do it. Yesterday's line: rejoice, pray, thank.

Every group chat has one: the person with opinions on everyone's business who somehow never finishes their own. A second letter to Thessalonica names that exact problem. Paul hears that some in the church are "working not at all, but are busybodies." Not idle and quiet. Busy, just not with their own work. Busy with everybody else's. So what's the cure? Paul's answer starts with a memory.
screen: `OPINIONS ON EVERYONE'S BUSINESS.` → `WORKING NOT AT ALL.` → `WHAT'S THE CURE?`

segments.voice: The memory: "Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you." Paul and his companions paid their own way, he says, to give the church an example. Then the line people still quote: "if any would not work, neither should he eat." Read the verb closely. Would not, not could not. It's about the able and unwilling, not the sick or anyone who can't find work. Then the cure itself: "that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread." Quietness here isn't silence. It's minding your own work without hovering over everyone else's. So that's Paul's answer: honest work, done quietly, is a kind of peace. A neighbor tradition prizes it too. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, Guru Nanak says that whoever eats what they earn by their own work, and gives some of it away, has recognized the path. Sikhs call honest work kirat karni. Shared ground: your own bread, earned honestly. One honest difference: the Guru's line ties earning straight to giving some away; Paul's lines here tie it to quiet, and to not being a burden. Then Paul turns to the tired ones doing it right: "But ye, brethren, be not weary in well doing." Even his correction stays gentle: the one who won't listen, he says, is not an enemy but a brother.
screen: `EAT NO MAN'S BREAD FOR NOUGHT.` · `WOULD NOT, NOT COULD NOT.` · `WITH QUIETNESS, YOUR OWN BREAD.` · `GURU NANAK: EARN, AND GIVE SOME AWAY.` · then, large: `BE NOT WEARY IN WELL DOING.`

segments.voice: Choose one piece of honest work that's yours today, a task nobody else will do for you. Name what finishing it well would look like, name the one thing most likely to pull you off it, and decide the first small step you'll take when the sit ends. Keep that step small enough to do without anyone noticing, which is rather the point.
Quietly working. Paul's word to the Thessalonians: do your own work, without noise or meddling, and eat your own bread.
Keep this one: be not weary in well doing, said to the ones already doing the work. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians see ordinary, honest work done well as part of their faith, and some monastic communities join daily prayer with daily work.

fork.setup: a classmate says 'if any would not work, neither should he eat' proves people who lose their jobs don't deserve help. what does the verse actually say?
options: would not: it's about the able and unwilling, not those who can't.
anyone without a job, for any reason, should go without.
it's about church leaders only, who shouldn't be paid at all.
fork.reveal: the King James says would not, not could not. Paul is writing about people able to work who became busybodies instead.
